titulo.en: I ask for, I repeat, I follow

objetivo.en: Say what you ask for, repeat, serve and follow in class and at work, using verbs that change e to i.

nota.en: Say “poo-PEE-treh”. A pupitre is the small desk a student sits at.
Say “ah-YOO-dah”: the y sounds like the y in “yes”.
Plural: las instrucciones. The ending -ción sounds like “SYOHN”.

traduccion.en: to ask for, to request, to order

nota.en: Pedir is to ask FOR something (help, coffee). To ask a question, Spanish uses preguntar.
The h is silent and the j is a strong h: “OH-hah”.

explicacion.en: Repetir changes its stem vowel: e becomes i in the forms yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ustedes. So it is repite, not repete.
The stem change also happens in the ellos/ustedes form: repiten, not repeten.
Do not use the e to ie change of verbs like querer here. Pedir, servir, repetir and seguir change e to i: repite.
The change to i does not happen in nosotros: pedimos, servimos, repetimos, seguimos.
In the yo form of seguir, the u disappears: sigo. In the other forms it stays: sigues, sigue, siguen.

titulo.en: Verbs that change e to i

texto.en: Four very useful verbs change the vowel e of their stem to i: pedir (to ask for), servir (to serve), repetir (to repeat) and seguir (to follow). The change happens when the stress falls on the stem, in yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes: pido, pides, pide, piden. In nosotros the stress moves to the ending, so the vowel stays: pedimos, servimos, repetimos, seguimos. You can picture a boot: every form changes except nosotros. Seguir also loses its u in the yo form: sigo, but sigues, sigue, siguen. Remember that pedir means to ask FOR something: pido ayuda, pido un café. To ask a question you use preguntar. Useful phrases: pedir ayuda, repetir la pregunta, seguir las instrucciones, servir café.

titulo.en: Tú or usted with these verbs

texto.en: The usted form is the same as the él/ella form: pide, sirve, repite, sigue. A student speaks to the teacher with usted: ¿Repite la pregunta, profesora? Emma uses usted with señora Rosa, so she asks ¿Sirve la sopa? and not ¿Sirves la sopa?. With Daniela, Mateo or Andrés she uses tú: ¿Repites la pregunta? To talk about several people, use ustedes with the same form as ellos: ustedes piden, ustedes siguen.
The stem changes in every form except nosotros. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: Do you know where it is? Do you know Andrés?

objetivo.en: Tell saber and conocer apart to talk about what you know and the people and places you know at work.

nota.en: The ñ sounds like “ny” in “canyon”. For a woman: la compañera.
Say “ehs-kree-TOH-ryoh”. The desk where you work, not the student's desk.
The y sounds like the y in “yes”: “proh-yehk-TOHR”. Keep the o short and pure.

traduccion.en: to know (a fact, or how to do something)
to know (a person or a place), to be familiar with

nota.en: Yo form: conozco. The z sounds like an s.

explicacion.en: For people you know, use conocer, not saber. Before a person you add the personal a: conozco a Andrés.
Before a specific person, Spanish needs the personal a: conozco a Andrés. Before a place there is no a: conozco Quito.
To know how to do something is saber + infinitive. Conocer is for people and places.
The yo form of saber is irregular: sé, not sabo.

texto.en: English uses “know” for everything, but Spanish has two verbs. Use saber for facts and information (sé dónde está la sala) and for knowing how to do something, followed by an infinitive (sé usar el proyector, ella sabe traducir). Use conocer for people and places, in the sense of being familiar with them: conozco a Andrés, conozco Quito. Before a specific person you need the personal a: conozco a Andrés, but conozco la oficina, with no a. In the yo form both verbs are irregular: sé (the accent tells it apart from se) and conozco. The same pattern appears in traducir: traduzco. All other forms are regular: sabes, sabe, sabemos, saben; conoces, conoce, conocemos, conocen.

To ask about information, combine saber with the question words you already know: ¿Sabes dónde está…? ¿Sabes quién es…? ¿Sabes cuándo es…? To ask whether someone knows a person, use ¿Conoces a…? With a stranger or an older person, use usted: ¿Sabe dónde está la oficina? ¿Conoce a Andrés? Use no sé to say you don't know a fact, and no conozco for a person or place you aren't familiar with.
Only the yo form is irregular. Tap each form to hear it.
Words you will meet in the examples and the dialogue.
Facts and abilities on the left, people and places on the right.

objetivo.en: Say what is happening right now at work and ask what another person is doing at this moment.

nota.en: The z sounds like an s: “TEE-sah”.
The first d is hard, the second one (between vowels) is soft, like the th in “this”.
Esperar a + a person means to wait for them: estoy esperando a Daniela.

explicacion.en: After estar you need the gerund (-ando, -iendo), not the infinitive: estoy escribiendo.
The gerund always needs a form of estar. By itself it is not a complete verb: Daniela está durmiendo.
Between two vowels the i becomes y: leer → leyendo, not leiendo.
Use estar, not ser, for an action in progress: estamos leyendo.
Seguir keeps its stem change in the gerund: e becomes i, so siguiendo, not seguiendo.

titulo.en: What is happening right now: estar + gerund

texto.en: To say what is happening at this very moment, Spanish uses estar + gerund, like English “to be” + -ing: estoy hablando (I am speaking), estás comiendo, está escribiendo. To form the gerund, take off the ending of the infinitive: -ar verbs add -ando (hablar → hablando) and -er/-ir verbs add -iendo (comer → comiendo, escribir → escribiendo). The gerund never changes for person or gender: estoy hablando, estamos hablando, están hablando. Time words you can add: ahora, ahora mismo, en este momento. The question is ¿Qué estás haciendo? (What are you doing?) and with usted ¿Qué está haciendo?

Some very common gerunds are spelled differently. When the ending -iendo falls between two vowels, the i becomes y: leer → leyendo. In -ir verbs that change their stem, the vowel changes in the gerund too: dormir → durmiendo (o becomes u), pedir → pidiendo and seguir → siguiendo (e becomes i). Do not use estar + gerund for plans in the future. English says “I'm leaving tomorrow”, but Spanish uses the simple present or another structure, not the gerund. The gerund is for actions that are in progress now.
Tap each phrase to hear it.

explicacion.en: In nosotros the o stays: solemos, like podemos or dormimos.

titulo.en: Soler + infinitive: what you usually do

texto.en: Soler + infinitive means to usually do something, to tend to do it. Suelo llegar a las ocho means “I usually arrive at eight”. Only soler changes for the person; the action verb stays in the infinitive. Soler changes its o to ue, like poder and dormir, in every form except nosotros: suelo, sueles, suele, solemos, suelen. For ustedes and ellos use suelen. To say what you usually do not do, put no before soler: no suelo trabajar los sábados. Add the time or the part of the day with a, por or en: suelo desayunar a las siete, suelo estudiar por la noche. In English “usually” is an adverb; in Spanish soler is a verb that needs an infinitive after it, so never say suelo llego.
The o becomes ue in every form except nosotros. Tap each form to hear it.

nota.en: The g before e sounds like a strong h: “heh-neh-rahl-MEHN-teh”.

explicacion.en: Start from the feminine form of the adjective: rápida + mente = rápidamente, with -a-, not -e-. Keep the accent too.
The written accent of the adjective stays in the adverb: fácil → fácilmente.
Do not use the masculine form. Use the feminine adjective: lenta + mente = lentamente.
The adverb of “good” is bien (well). It does not end in -mente, and you don't use the adjective buena to describe how someone does something.

titulo.en: Adverbs in -mente: how to form them

texto.en: Many Spanish adverbs of manner end in -mente, like English adverbs in -ly. Take the feminine singular form of the adjective and add -mente: rápida → rápidamente (quickly), lenta → lentamente (slowly), clara → claramente (clearly), tranquila → tranquilamente (calmly). Adjectives that have only one form, ending in -e or in a consonant, do not change: normal → normalmente, general → generalmente, frecuente → frecuentemente, fácil → fácilmente. If the adjective has a written accent, the accent stays: fácil → fácilmente, rápida → rápidamente. In speech the adverb keeps both stresses, one on the adjective and one on -mente.

Adverbs of time like normalmente, generalmente and frecuentemente usually go at the beginning of the sentence: Normalmente llego a las ocho. Adverbs of manner like rápidamente, lentamente, claramente or tranquilamente usually go after the verb: Sofía explica claramente. Trabajo tranquilamente. The adverb never changes for gender or number. Remember one exception: the adverb of “good” is bien, not an adverb in -mente. Use these adverbs with the time expressions you know: Normalmente empiezo a las ocho, Generalmente salgo a las cinco.

contexto.en: Andrés Vaca is preparing the team's schedule for the term and asks Emma about hers. They use tú.

dialogo.texto: Emma, ¿cuál es tu horario?
Este año generalmente tengo clase de lunes a jueves, por la mañana, de ocho a doce. Los viernes no tengo clase.

traduccion.en: This year I generally have class from Monday to Thursday, in the morning, from eight to twelve. On Fridays I have no class.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y a qué hora almuerzas?

traduccion.en: And what time do you have lunch?

dialogo.texto: Normalmente almuerzo a la una. Por la tarde estoy en la oficina.

traduccion.en: Normally I have lunch at one. In the afternoon I am in the office.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y la reunión del equipo? ¿Cuándo es?

traduccion.en: And the team meeting? When is it?

dialogo.texto: Es el viernes a las diez. Sofía explica claramente y trabaja tranquilamente.

traduccion.en: It is on Friday at ten. Sofía explains clearly and works calmly.

dialogo.texto: Muy bien, gracias. Yo frecuentemente salgo a las seis. ¿Y tú?

traduccion.en: Very good, thank you. I often leave at six. And you?

dialogo.texto: Generalmente salgo a las cinco. ¡Qué bien! Hasta luego, Andrés.

traduccion.en: Generally I leave at five. Great! See you later, Andrés.
